A Rust service is one of the easiest things to deploy: a single static binary, no interpreter, no node_modules. This module covers containerising it properly and running it in production.

The multi-stage Dockerfile

Choice Why
--locked fails the build if Cargo.lock would change
non-root user container escape is much less useful as uid 10001
ca-certificates TLS to Postgres/APIs needs a trust store
no cargo build of tests halves build time
debian:bookworm-slim runtime glibc present, ~75 MB

Distroless / scratch, and static builds

Result: a ~10 MB image with no shell, no package manager, and almost no attack surface. Note that sqlx::migrate! embeds your migrations, so there is no file to copy.

Gotcha: with scratch there is no /etc/passwd, no ca-certificates, and no timezone database. Use distroless/static (it includes certs) rather than bare scratch unless you have checked every dependency.

Build cache that actually works

Without this dance, every source change re-downloads and re-compiles all ~300 dependencies. It turns a 6-minute CI build into 40 seconds.

Docker Compose for local development

Configuration

Twelve-factor: everything from the environment, nothing baked into the image.

Fail fast and loudly on a missing required variable — a container that starts and then 500s on every request is worse than one that refuses to start.

Migrations in production

Three approaches, in order of preference:

  1. A separate migration job that runs before the deployment and must succeed. Cleanest: the API never blocks on DDL, and a failed migration stops the deploy.
  2. At API startup (sqlx::migrate!().run()) — simple, but with N replicas they all race. sqlx takes an advisory lock so it is safe, just serialised.
  3. Manually — only acceptable for a single-instance service.

Gotcha: a migration that takes 4 minutes on a large table will hold the advisory lock and block every starting replica. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (outside a transaction) and add columns as nullable first.

Zero-downtime deploys

The requirements:

  1. Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM — drain in-flight requests. (Already wired in module 05.02.)
  2. Readiness probe returns 503 while shutting down, so the load balancer stops sending traffic before the process exits.
  3. Long enough terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain (30–60 s).

Kubernetes essentials

maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 means capacity never drops during a rollout. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is possible because the binary writes nothing to disk — a Rust service has no temp files by default.

Memory limits deserve a note: Rust has no GC, so RSS is stable and predictable. Set the limit ~2× steady-state RSS and you will not see OOM kills. That predictability is one of the better operational arguments for Rust.

Observability in production

Ship /metrics to Prometheus. Alert on:

Alert Condition
Error rate 5xx > 1% for 5 min
Latency p99 > 1 s for 5 min
Saturation DB pool in-use > 90% for 5 min
Queue stuck jobs_pending rising for 10 min
Crash loop restart count > 3 in 10 min

The frontend

Enable output: "standalone" in next.config.ts for a ~120 MB image instead of ~1 GB. Deploy it to Vercel if you can — it is less work and the Next.js build pipeline is tuned for it.

Release checklist

  • cargo clippy -- -D warnings clean
  • cargo test --workspace and cargo test --doc green
  • cargo audit and cargo deny check clean
  • npm run typecheck and npm run build green
  • Migrations reviewed, and reversible or additive-only
  • Image tagged with a version, never latest
  • /healthz and /readyz respond correctly
  • Graceful shutdown verified (docker stop takes ~2 s, not 10)
  • Rollback plan: previous image tag is one command away
  • Dashboards and alerts exist before the deploy, not after

Exercises

  1. Build the multi-stage image and compare its size against a naive single-stage build.
  2. Add the dependency-caching layer and measure the rebuild time after touching one .rs file.
  3. Switch to distroless/static and confirm TLS to Postgres still works.
  4. Verify graceful shutdown: start a 5-second request, docker stop, and confirm it completes.
  5. Make /readyz return 503 during shutdown and observe the load balancer behaviour.
  6. Write the Compose file and get the full stack (Postgres + API + worker + web) running with one command.
